artworks.title: Hector Taking Leave of Andromache: the Fright of Astyanax
artworks.description: West's engraving freezes Iliad 6: the infant Astyanax shrinks from Hector's crested helmet as Andromache holds him — the child already named 'lord of the city' in the moment his father rides out to die.

artworks.title: Hector Holding Astyanax
artworks.description: Carpeaux's sculpture groups father and son: Hector cradles Astyanax — the Trojan heir as a small body against the warrior who alone, Homer says, guarded Ilios.

artworks.title: Neoptolemus and Astyanax
artworks.description: A late Mannerist bronze stages the sack's cruel close: Neoptolemus seizes the child Astyanax — the death from the walls that ends Hector's line in the Little Iliad tradition.

artworks.title: Child Murder (Mykonos Vase, detail)
artworks.description: On the Mykonos pithos that first shows the Trojan Horse, Greek warriors tear children from the city — among the earliest images of the sack's infant killings that later name Astyanax.

popCulture.title: Andromaque
popCulture.creator: Jean Racine
popCulture.description: Racine's tragedy turns on Astyanax as the living stake: Andromache must choose between Pyrrhus and her son's life — Hector's child as the hinge of French classical pathos.

popCulture.title: The Trojan Women
popCulture.creator: Euripides
popCulture.description: Euripides makes Astyanax's death the play's quiet atrocity: Talthybius takes the child from Andromache to be thrown from the walls — the infant heir as the last Trojan loss.

popCulture.title: Astyanax
popCulture.description: Hector and Andromache's son — Scamandrius at home, Astyanax to the people — whose fall from the walls closes the city's future.
